stimulus.text: Historian Joseph Ellis writes that the early republic was 'an extended argument about what the Revolution had actually meant' — with the Constitution's silences over federal versus state power guaranteeing that every crisis became a constitutional debate.

parts: A. Briefly explain ONE example of debate over constitutional principles in the United States in the period 1787–1800.
B. Briefly explain a SECOND example of such debate in the same period.
C. Briefly explain ONE example of a political leader acting on constitutional principle in this period.
exemplar: At the 1787 Constitutional Convention, delegates clashed over representation: large states wanted proportional representation while small states demanded equality. The Great Compromise created a Senate with two senators per state and a House apportioned by population.
In 1798 Jefferson and Madison protested the Alien and Sedition Acts with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, arguing that states could refuse to enforce federal laws they deemed unconstitutional.

President Washington defended the Constitution's treaty process in 1796 by refusing the House's demand for the Jay Treaty papers, insisting that treaty-making belonged to the president and Senate — putting constitutional principle above political convenience.

stimulus.text: "Behold, then, the unlettered man of the West, the nursling of the wilds, the farmer of the Hermitage … raised by the people to the highest pinnacle of honor … he came as one free from the bonds of hereditary or established custom; he came with no superior but conscience, nor oracle but his native judgment … he valued right more than usage." —George Bancroft, Eulogy on Andrew Jackson, 1845 (abridged)

parts: A. Briefly describe Bancroft's assessment of Andrew Jackson.
B. Briefly explain ONE historical event or development that supports Bancroft's assessment.
C. Briefly explain the perspective of someone opposed to Bancroft's assessment of Jackson.
exemplar: Bancroft portrays Jackson as the embodiment of the democratic West: a natural, uncorrupted man of the people who valued principle over established custom and Eastern corruption.
Jackson's veto of the Bank of the United States supports Bancroft's view: Jackson presented it as a stand for ordinary people against a privileged Eastern financial elite.
Whig opponents saw Jackson as a dangerous demagogue: they called him 'King Andrew,' condemned his use of the veto and patronage, and denounced the forced removal of Native peoples as tyrannical.

stimulus.attribution: Described from the 1870 commemorative print 'The Fifteenth Amendment. Celebrated May 19th, 1870' (Library of Congress).
stimulus.text: The large commemorative print celebrates the Fifteenth Amendment: at center, a grand parade with uniformed Black troops, marching bands, and cheering crowds winds past a speaker's stand; around the border, portrait medallions of Grant, Lincoln, and others frame smaller scenes of Black life as full citizens - men casting ballots, a wedding, children in a schoolroom, legislators at work. American flags drape the composition.

parts: A. Briefly explain the point of view expressed in the cartoon about voting rights.
B. Briefly explain how one visual element of the cartoon supports your answer to part A.
C. Briefly explain one way in which the right depicted in the cartoon was challenged between 1866 and 1896.
exemplar: The print celebrates Black suffrage under the Fifteenth Amendment, presenting the Black voter as a dignified citizen whose rights have been nationally vindicated - enfranchisement as triumph, not controversy.
The surrounding vignettes show Black men voting, holding office, and sending children to school, depicting suffrage as the gateway to full, respectable citizenship.
Southern states used violence, poll taxes, and literacy tests to strip Black men of the vote, and the Supreme Court weakened federal enforcement in United States v. Cruikshank (1876).
